theoryAdd.text: Going Deeper: Object Lifetime, Copies and Clean-up

Every object's life is bracketed by exactly one constructor call and, unless it is leaked, one destructor call. Where the object lives decides when its constructor runs: a local object at its definition, a global object before main() starts, a static local object the first time control passes its definition, a heap object at new, and a temporary where the expression creates it. Destruction mirrors this: locals die at the closing brace of their block, temporaries at the end of the full expression (the semicolon), heap objects only at delete, and static and global objects after main() returns, last constructed first destroyed. Inside one object, member objects are constructed in declaration order before the constructor body runs, and destroyed in the reverse order after the destructor body.

theoryAdd.text: The copy constructor runs whenever a new object is initialised from an existing one: T b = a;, T b(a);, T b{a};, and passing an object to a function by value. Since C++17, initialising an object from a temporary of the same type builds it in place, so T x = T(5); and return T(5); call only T(int) and no copy constructor. Returning a named local object may also skip the copy (named return value optimisation), so textbook counts that include that copy can differ from what a real compiler prints. Assignment a = b; between two existing objects never calls a constructor; it calls operator=.

Buf a(1)  : a.p -> new int holding 1
Buf b = a : the copy constructor gives b its own int (1)  -> "copy "
Buf c(9)  : c.p -> new int holding 9
c = a     : operator= copies the value 1 into c's int     -> "assign "
*a.p = 5  : only a's int changes; b and c still hold 1
Output: copy assign 511
With the compiler's shallow versions, all three p would hold one
address: the line would print 555 and the three destructors would then
delete one int three times, which is undefined behaviour.

theoryAdd.text: Traps in constructor and destructor questions:
items: Members are initialised in the order they are declared in the class, whatever order the initialiser list uses; a member initialised from a later-declared member reads an uninitialised value.
A constructor whose parameters all have defaults, such as W(int x = 5), is also a default constructor, so declaring W() as well makes W w; ambiguous.
explicit on a one-argument constructor blocks T t = 5; and calls such as f(5) that need an implicit conversion, while T t(5); and T t = T(5); still compile.
T(4); on its own line creates and immediately destroys a temporary, so its constructor and destructor output appear together at that point.
A static local object is constructed only on the first call and destroyed after main() returns, not at the end of each call.
An object created with new whose pointer is lost is never destroyed, so its destructor output never appears; every new[] also needs delete[].

theoryAdd.text: Never let two objects own the same heap block. If a class has a destructor that deletes a pointer member, the compiler's shallow copy constructor and assignment make two objects delete one block, which is undefined behaviour. Either write all three members (rule of three) or forbid copying with T(const T &) = delete;.

questions.explanation: p is created with the default constructor (v = 1) and q with the parameterised constructor (v = 7), so 1 + 7 = 8 is printed.

questions.questionText: In C++, a default constructor is a constructor that:
options: Is always generated by the compiler and never written by the programmer
Can be called without any arguments
Takes a reference to an object of the same class
questions.explanation: A default constructor is any constructor that can be called with no arguments: one with no parameters, or one whose parameters all have default values. The programmer may write it, a copy constructor is the one taking a reference, and constructors have no return type.

questions.questionText: When does the compiler implicitly declare a default constructor for a class?
options: Always, even when the class declares other constructors
Only when the class has no data members
Only when the class declares no constructor of its own
Only when the class also declares a destructor
questions.explanation: The implicit default constructor is provided only if the class declares no constructor at all. As soon as any constructor such as B(int) is written, B b; needs a user-written default constructor.
Declaring B(int) stops the compiler from supplying a default constructor, so B b; (line 2) has no matching constructor. Lines 1 and 3 both call B(int).

questions.questionText: Defining several constructors in one class that differ in the number or types of their parameters is called:
questions.explanation: Several constructors with different parameter lists in one class is constructor overloading; the arguments given when an object is created select one of them. Overriding refers to virtual functions redefined in a derived class.

questions.questionText: What is the essential difference between Box *p = new Box; and Box *q = (Box *) malloc(sizeof(Box)); ?
options: malloc runs Box's constructor, but new does not
new allocates memory and then runs Box's constructor; malloc only allocates raw, unconstructed memory
Both run the constructor; only the syntax differs
new allocates the object on the stack and malloc on the heap
questions.explanation: new obtains memory and then runs the constructor, returning a typed Box*; malloc returns raw memory of the requested size and never runs a constructor. Both allocate from the free store (heap).

questions.questionText: What is meant by a dynamic constructor in C++?
options: A constructor that allocates memory with new while the object is being created, so that each object can get storage of the size it needs
A constructor declared virtual, so that the version to be called is chosen at run time
The default constructor that the compiler generates when a class declares no constructor
A constructor that runs only for objects created with new, never for local objects
questions.explanation: Allocating memory for an object's data at the moment the object is constructed is called dynamic construction: for example Str(const char *s) { len = strlen(s); p = new char[len + 1]; strcpy(p, s); }, with a destructor that frees p using delete[]. It runs for local and heap objects alike, and a constructor can never be declared virtual.

questions.questionText: sizeof(Box) is 12 bytes. For the statement Box *p = new Box[5]; how many bytes are needed for the objects, and how many times does Box's default constructor run?
questions.explanation: new Box[5] needs 5 × 12 = 60 bytes for the objects (an implementation may add a little bookkeeping space) and runs the default constructor once per element, 5 times.

questions.questionText: What happens when delete is applied to a pointer whose value is nullptr?
options: The program crashes with an access violation
Compile error: delete needs a non-null pointer
Nothing happens; deleting a null pointer is a safe no-op
questions.explanation: The language defines delete on a null pointer as doing nothing. That is why setting a pointer to nullptr after deleting it makes an accidental second delete harmless.

questions.questionText: A class declares no copy constructor. What does the copy constructor supplied by the compiler do?
options: It copies each data member in turn (member-wise copy), so a pointer member of the copy points to the same memory as the original
It allocates new heap memory for every pointer member and copies the pointed-to data (deep copy)
It copies only the public data members
Nothing: copying an object of such a class is a compile error
questions.explanation: The implicit copy constructor copies each member in turn (a member-wise, shallow copy): a pointer is copied as an address, not the memory it points to. Classes that own heap memory therefore need their own deep-copying version.

questions.questionText: Which of the following can NOT be declared virtual in C++?
questions.explanation: A constructor builds an object whose exact type must already be known, so constructors cannot be virtual. Destructors, ordinary member functions and operator functions can all be virtual.

questions.explanation: Missing trailing arguments take their defaults: x is 2 × 3 = 6, y is 4 × 3 = 12 and z is 4 × 5 = 20, so 6 + 12 + 20 = 38. A constructor whose parameters all have defaults also serves as the default constructor.

Member objects are constructed before the constructor body runs, and Eng has no default constructor, so e must receive its argument in the initialiser list. Every other version would first need Eng().

questions.explanation: D() delegates to D(7), which delegates to D(7, 7) (C++11 delegating constructors). The target constructor finishes before the delegating one's body runs, so the bodies print 2, then 1, then 0.

An explicit constructor cannot be used for implicit conversions, so the copy-initialisation E b = 2 and the call take(4), which would convert 4 to E, are rejected. Direct initialisation E a(1) and the explicit E(3) are allowed.

options: Compile error: the constructor is private, so main() cannot create a Logger object
It compiles, because constructors are always accessible
It compiles, because the compiler adds a public default constructor
It compiles, but creating g throws an exception at run time
questions.explanation: A private constructor can be called only by the class's own members and friends, so Logger g; in main() is rejected. This is how classes such as singletons control where objects are created.

Creating a prints D. Passing a by value to f makes a copy (K) that is destroyed when the call ends (X); g takes a reference, so no copy is made, and a is destroyed at the end of main (X).

questions.questionText: Why is the parameter of a copy constructor normally declared as const Box & rather than Box &?
options: Because a copy constructor with a non-const reference parameter is not allowed
So that const objects can also be copied, and the object being copied cannot be modified by mistake
Because const makes the copy run faster
Because const turns the copy constructor into a default constructor
questions.explanation: Box(Box &) is a legal copy constructor, but it cannot accept a const Box, and it would allow the source to be changed. const Box & accepts both const and non-const objects and promises not to modify them.

options: Compile error: S has no copy constructor
questions.explanation: The compiler-generated copy constructor copies the pointer value, so a.p and b.p point to the same int. Writing 9 through b.p is therefore seen through a.p.

options: Each object frees its own separate array, and the program ends normally
Both destructors delete[] the same array, which is undefined behaviour (often a crash)
Compile error: Buf needs a user-written copy constructor
Only a's destructor runs, because b is just a copy
questions.explanation: The implicit copy constructor copies the pointer, so a and b refer to the same array. At the end of main both destructors delete[] it, and freeing one block twice is undefined behaviour.

questions.questionText: A class allocates memory with new in its constructor and frees it in a user-written destructor. According to the rule of three, which two other members should it normally also define?
options: The default constructor and a parameterised constructor
A friend function and a static member function
The copy constructor and the copy assignment operator
A virtual function and a conversion operator
questions.explanation: Rule of three: a class that needs a user-written destructor to release a resource almost always needs a user-written copy constructor and copy assignment operator too, so that copies neither share nor leak that resource.
a and b are built in order; c is built and destroyed inside the inner block; d is built next. At the end of main the remaining locals die in reverse order of construction: d, b, a.
The member object m is constructed before the body of Out's constructor runs, and destroyed after the body of Out's destructor has finished: i, o, ~o, ~i.
